newsitem.title: USA: FAA approves Boeing 777, GE engines on long routes.
newsitem.headline: FAA approves Boeing 777, GE engines on long routes.

text.p: The Federal Aviation Administration Thursday granted approval for Boeing Co.'s 777 jetliner powered by General Electric Co. engines to operate on long, over-water routes.
Similar approval for extended-range twin-engine operations, or ETOPS, previously had been granted for 777 models powered by Pratt & Whitney engines.

Without such approval, the twin-engine jets cannot fly further than 60 minutes from the nearest airport, forcing airlines to take less direct routes closer to land and eliminating long-distance journeys to destinations such as Hawaii.
The FAA move culminates a series of tests in which the airplane took off and landed 1,000 times after the GE90 engine had been tested extensively on the ground and in computer simulations.

Earlier problems with the engines, including a failed bird-strike test, contributed to a delay in the initial 777 delivery last year to British Airways Plc, but FAA administrator David Hinson said the testing had proven the airworthiness of the jet.
"The GE90 engine performed nearly flawlessly," Hinson said in a statement.
Following expected approval by Europe's Joint Airworthiness Authority, British Airways is expected be the first to take advantage of the new rating.
Boeing said 37 of the 777 models have been delivered to eight customers worldwide and another 244 are on order.

The wide-body jet also also is available with Rolls-Royce Plc engines, which do not have extended-range clearance yet. A Boeing spokesman said the 777 with Rolls-Royce engines is expected to win approval for ETOPS soon.
